title: Short Stuff: SINA
summary: Short Stuff episode on SINA (the Society for Indecency to Naked Animals), a 1950s-60s hoax created by writer-hoaxer Alan Abel. Josh and Chuck recount how a fake group campaigning to clothe animals drew around 50,000 members after a 1959 Today Show appearance by its fictitious president "G. Clifford Prute Jr.", played by Buck Henry. The hoax peaked with a 1962 CBS News interview with Walter Cronkite, where the fake president sang the anthem "Wings of Decency" on ukulele. The hoax was exposed by Time magazine in 1964. Abel's motive was mocking 1950s moral stuffiness, inspired by a Texas highway incident with two cows mating. The hosts close with a discussion of clothing pets and a ThunderCats tangent.
topics: Society for Indecency to Naked Animals

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to SINA
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter and introduce SINA, a group formed to clothe animals and considered a prime example of 1950s stodgy morality. Josh describes its founding goals and the 1959 Today Show appearance by its president.

segments.title: SINA's growth and membership campaign
segments.summary: The hosts describe how SINA's president called for clothing all animals, said zoos were peep shows, and how membership swelled to about 50,000 after the Today Show appearance. Members were encouraged to issue summonses to neighbors, picket the White House, and write to President Kennedy.

segments.title: CBS interview with Walter Cronkite and the anthem
segments.summary: In 1962, the fake president appeared on CBS News with Walter Cronkite and sang the anthem 'Wings of Decency' on ukulele. A CBS cameraman recognized the man as Buck Henry, who would later become a famous screenwriter and actor.

segments.title: Alan Abel's hoax and its origins
segments.summary: The hosts explain that Clifford Prute was a fabrication by hoaxer Alan Abel, played by Buck Henry. Abel's motive was mocking 1950s moral stuffiness, inspired by a Texas highway incident with two cows. A letter to the Saturday Evening Post was rejected, which prompted Abel to recruit Henry. The hoax ran for years and was exposed by Time magazine in 1964.

segments.title: Hoax legacy and no money taken
segments.summary: The hosts note that no money was taken from members, including the unused $40,000 check, and that the hoax accidentally created a real movement. They reflect on it as a cultural criticism.

segments.title: Pet clothing tangent and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss their views on dressing pets, with Josh saying warm sweaters are fine but fashion-only outfits are not respectful. They tangent to ThunderCats and close with credits and sources.
